cards.interpretation: In AML, pretransplant MRD positivity is not a contraindication to allogeneic HCT; transplantation may improve outcome compared with continued chemotherapy or observation in MRD-positive patients.

In FLT3-ITD AML after allogeneic HCT, gilteritinib maintenance is recommended for patients with FLT3-ITD UHS-NGS MRD positivity before and/or after transplant.
For AML patients receiving standard-of-care FLT3-inhibitor maintenance, evidence is currently very limited for stopping treatment on the basis of MRD results.
In AML treated with a hypomethylating agent plus venetoclax, mutated-NPM1 qPCR MRD is prognostic; its clinical utility in this setting remains under investigation.

cards.interpretation: Before using a rare NPM1 variant, very large FLT3-ITD, or uncommon noncanonical PML::RARA transcript as an AML MRD marker, analyte detectability should be confirmed at diagnosis with the intended MRD assay.

For mutated-NPM1 AML, MRD levels are approximately tenfold higher in bone marrow than peripheral blood; MRD negativity is defined as <0.001% NPM1/ABL1 or by the EAC criterion with at least 10,000 ABL1 copies, and MRD-LL thresholds therefore differ by tissue.

After two chemotherapy cycles in mutated-NPM1 AML, formal qPCR MRD positivity is defined in peripheral blood rather than bone marrow because bone-marrow positivity does not sufficiently discriminate risk; a positive peripheral-blood result is classified as warning rather than high risk of treatment failure.

At end of treatment in mutated-NPM1 AML, the recommended bone-marrow NPM1/ABL1 positivity threshold is 0.1%; this threshold has prognostic significance and replaces the former 2% threshold, which often identifies patients already near hematologic relapse.

For RUNX1::RUNX1T1 or CBFB::MYH11 AML, a ≥3-log reduction from diagnostic baseline is recommended to stratify relapse risk; log reduction should be measured in the same tissue, bone marrow is preferred, and a diagnostic transcript baseline is required.

In RUNX1::RUNX1T1 or CBFB::MYH11 AML, low-level fusion-transcript persistence at end of treatment can occur without subsequent relapse; MRD-relapse thresholds were therefore redefined to reduce overtreatment of low-risk MRD-LL persistence.

In PML::RARA APL, MRD monitoring is recommended at end of treatment rather than during ongoing treatment; end-of-treatment positivity is a warning because transient stable MRD-LL can occur, and follow-up should document stability or conversion to MRD negativity.

For FLT3-ITD AML, UHS-NGS MRD is recommended after two treatment cycles and before allogeneic HCT; end-of-treatment and follow-up monitoring are recommended on more limited evidence, and positivity is defined as greater than the assay LOD with LOD at least 0.01% VAF.
In AML with both mutated NPM1 and FLT3-ITD, mutated-NPM1 MRD can serve as a stand-alone marker when FLT3-ITD UHS-NGS is unavailable.
In AML with both mutated NPM1 and FLT3-ITD, persistence of MRD by either mutated-NPM1 qPCR or FLT3-ITD UHS-NGS is associated with increased risk compared with negativity by both markers.

After two intensive-chemotherapy cycles or before allogeneic HCT, peripheral-blood mutated-NPM1 qPCR is optimal when <0.001% or undetectable, warning/MRD-LL at detectable 0.001% to <0.01%, and warning/MRD-positive at detectable ≥0.01%.

cards.interpretation: CHIP is defined by a somatic mutation in a myeloid malignancy-associated gene detected in blood or marrow at VAF ≥2% (≥4% for X-linked mutations in males), in a person without a diagnosed haematologic disorder or unexplained cytopenia.
CCUS is CHIP accompanied by one or more persistent otherwise-unexplained cytopenias that do not meet diagnostic criteria for a defined myeloid neoplasm.
For CCUS, MDS and MDS/MPN, cytopenia thresholds are haemoglobin <13 g/dL in males or <12 g/dL in females, ANC <1.8 ×10^9/L, and platelets <150 ×10^9/L.
CML is defined by the BCR::ABL1 fusion resulting from t(9;22)(q34;q11).
In CML, ABL1 kinase mutations are described as a source of TKI resistance and a key disease attribute in the current classification.
CML blast phase is defined by ≥20% myeloid blasts in blood or marrow, extramedullary blast proliferation, or increased lymphoblasts in blood or marrow; accelerated phase is omitted from WHO5.
Major PV diagnostic criteria include elevated haemoglobin and/or haematocrit, marrow panmyelosis with pleomorphic mature megakaryocytes, and JAK2 p.V617F or a JAK2 exon 12 mutation.
In PMF, mutations in EZH2, IDH1, IDH2, SRSF2, U2AF1 and ASXL1 are associated with poorer prognostic risk.
CNL is a BCR::ABL1-negative MPN characterized by sustained neutrophilia with WBC ≥25 ×10^9/L and ≥80% segmented neutrophils/bands, neutrophilic marrow hypercellularity and hepatosplenomegaly.
CEL is characterized by sustained clonal proliferation of morphologically abnormal eosinophils/eosinophil precursors causing persistent blood and marrow hypereosinophilia.
For CEL, the interval required to define sustained hypereosinophilia is 4 weeks rather than 6 months.
CEL requires both evidence of clonality and abnormal bone-marrow morphology, such as megakaryocytic or erythroid dysplasia.
For CEL, increased blasts (≥2% in blood or 5–19% in marrow) are no longer an alternative to demonstrating clonality.
Updated JMML criteria require exclusion of KMT2A rearrangements.
JMML diagnosis emphasizes molecular studies demonstrating RAS-pathway activation together with clinical and laboratory criteria.
JMML initiated by somatic PTPN11 mutations is among the most aggressive genetic types.
A subset of JMML is associated with pathogenic germline CBL variants.
JMML associated with pathogenic germline CBL variants can occasionally undergo spontaneous remission.
In systemic mastocytosis, KIT p.D816V with VAF ≥10% in bone-marrow cells or peripheral-blood leukocytes qualifies as a B-finding.
Any KIT mutation causing ligand-independent activation is accepted as a minor diagnostic criterion for systemic mastocytosis.
Well-differentiated systemic mastocytosis may occur in any systemic-mastocytosis subtype; most cases lack KIT codon 816 mutation and typically show CD25/CD2 negativity with CD30 positivity.
MDS is defined by cytopenias and morphologic dysplasia, with a recommended dysplasia threshold of 10% for all lineages.
Within genetically defined MDS, MDS with biallelic TP53 inactivation supersedes MDS-5q and MDS-SF3B1 in the WHO5 hierarchy.
In MDS-5q, an SF3B1 mutation or a TP53 mutation that is not multi-hit does not by itself override the MDS-5q diagnosis.
For SF3B1-wild-type MDS with ≥15% ring sideroblasts, “MDS with low blasts and ring sideroblasts” remains an acceptable alternative designation.

Clinical assessment of biallelic TP53 alterations in MDS uses sequencing covering at least exons 4–11 together with copy-number assessment; TP53 locus loss may also be inferred by next-generation sequencing.
In MDS, TP53 VAF ≥50% may be regarded as presumptive, but not definitive, evidence of trans-allelic copy loss or copy-neutral LOH when a constitutional TP53 variant has been ruled out.
When two or more TP53 mutations are detected in MDS, they usually affect both alleles and may be considered multi-hit status.
MDS with biallelic TP53 alterations is regarded as very high risk in IPSS-R and is usually associated with complex or very complex karyotype.
Published data support considering MDS with biallelic TP53 inactivation as AML-equivalent for therapeutic purposes.
Pathogenic germline GATA2 or DDX41 variants can present with hypoplastic marrow and evolve to MDS and/or AML.
In the hypoplastic-marrow differential, individuals with germline GATA2 or DDX41 pathogenic variants are described as not responding to immunosuppressive treatment.
WHO5 retains a 20% blast cutoff to delineate MDS from AML while removing blast cutoffs for most AML types with defining genetic abnormalities.
MDS-IB2 may be regarded as AML-equivalent for therapeutic considerations and, when appropriate, clinical-trial design.

In childhood MDS with low blasts, monosomy 7, 7q deletion, or complex karyotype is associated with increased risk of AML progression and is typically treated with haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation.
CMML requires persistent absolute peripheral-blood monocytosis ≥0.5 ×10^9/L and relative monocytosis ≥10%.
When absolute monocytosis is ≥0.5 but <1.0 ×10^9/L, CMML diagnosis requires a clonal cytogenetic or molecular abnormality and dysplasia in at least one lineage.
In a patient with monocytosis, a documented MPN history excludes CMML; marrow MPN features and/or a high burden of JAK2, CALR or MPL mutations supports MPN with monocytosis rather than CMML.

In a suspected CMML case with eosinophilia, myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with tyrosine-kinase gene fusions should be excluded by assessing for PDGFRA rearrangement (most commonly FIP1L1::PDGFRA), PDGFRB rearrangement (most commonly ETV6::PDGFRB), FGFR1 rearrangement, JAK2 rearrangement, FLT3 rearrangement, ETV6::ABL1, and other defined tyrosine-kinase fusions including ETV6::FGFR2, ETV6::LYN, ETV6::NTRK3, RANBP2::ALK, BCR::RET, and FGFR1OP::RET. WHO5 treats PDGFRA, PDGFRB, FGFR1, JAK2 and FLT3 as rearrangement-defined categories rather than restricting them to a single fusion partner.

AML, myelodysplasia-related has a mutation-based definition that includes SRSF2, SF3B1, U2AF1, ZRSR2, ASXL1, EZH2, BCOR or STAG2.
Morphologic myelodysplasia alone is no longer sufficient to diagnose AML, myelodysplasia-related.
In acute megakaryoblastic leukaemia, the RAM immunophenotype correlates with CBFA2T3::GLIS2, a subtype of AML with other defined genetic alterations.
KIT mutations remain relevant prognostic factors in the genetically defined AML context discussed by WHO5.
WHO5 emphasizes the increased importance of highly sensitive MRD evaluation techniques in the genetically defined AML context of PML::RARA and RUNX1::RUNX1T1.
Post-induction MRD status is a prognostic factor in the genetically defined AML context discussed for PML::RARA and RUNX1::RUNX1T1 AML.

In AML or MDS after cytotoxic therapy, outcomes are generally worse with biallelic/multi-hit TP53 alterations, including ≥2 TP53 mutations or a TP53 mutation with 17p/TP53 deletion or copy-neutral LOH.
In myeloid neoplasms after cytotoxic therapy, PPM1D and other DNA-damage-response gene mutations may warrant additional work-up for germline predisposition.
A germline pathogenic/likely pathogenic CEBPA variant is recognized as CEBPA-associated familial AML within myeloid neoplasms with germline predisposition.
A germline pathogenic/likely pathogenic DDX41 variant is a recognized myeloid-neoplasm predisposition subtype.
A germline pathogenic/likely pathogenic TP53 variant (Li-Fraumeni syndrome) is a recognized myeloid-neoplasm predisposition subtype.
A germline pathogenic/likely pathogenic RUNX1 variant defines familial platelet disorder with associated myeloid malignancy.
A germline pathogenic/likely pathogenic ANKRD26 variant (Thrombocytopenia 2) is recognized among myeloid neoplasms with germline predisposition and a pre-existing platelet disorder.
A germline pathogenic/likely pathogenic ETV6 variant (Thrombocytopenia 5) is recognized among myeloid neoplasms with germline predisposition and a pre-existing platelet disorder.
A germline pathogenic/likely pathogenic GATA2 variant (GATA2 deficiency) is recognized among myeloid neoplasms with germline predisposition and potential organ dysfunction.
CBL syndrome is included among RASopathies associated with myeloid-neoplasm germline predisposition.
A germline pathogenic/likely pathogenic SAMD9 variant (MIRAGE syndrome) is a recognized myeloid-neoplasm predisposition state.
A germline pathogenic/likely pathogenic SAMD9L variant is recognized in SAMD9L-related ataxia-pancytopenia syndrome; ataxia is not always present.
Biallelic germline pathogenic/likely pathogenic BLM variants (Bloom syndrome) are a recognized myeloid-neoplasm predisposition state.
Before a diagnosis of CEL is rendered, myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with tyrosine-kinase gene fusions must be excluded.
For MLN-TK with PDGFRA or PDGFRB rearrangement, TKI therapy—particularly imatinib—has dramatically altered the natural history.
MLN-TK with FGFR1, JAK2 or FLT3 fusions or ETV6::ABL1 has more variable sensitivity to available newer-generation TKIs.
For MLN-TK with FGFR1, JAK2 or FLT3 fusions or ETV6::ABL1, long-term disease-free survival may in most cases require allogeneic haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation.
WHO5 lists mixed-phenotype acute leukaemia with BCR::ABL1 fusion and with KMT2A rearrangement among acute leukaemias of ambiguous lineage with defining genetic abnormalities.
MPAL with ZNF384 rearrangement is a WHO5 subtype of acute leukaemia with a defining genetic alteration and commonly has a B/myeloid immunophenotype.
Acute leukaemia of ambiguous lineage with BCL11B rearrangement is a WHO5 subtype with a defining genetic alteration and may occur with heterogeneous immunophenotypes.
For flow-cytometric MPO assessment in acute leukaemia, a >10% positivity threshold appears to improve specificity over 3%, but WHO5 states that no consensus cutoff has been established.
BPDCN immunophenotypic diagnosis requires either CD123 plus one other pDC marker with CD4 and/or CD56, or any three pDC markers with absence of all expected negative markers.

cards.interpretation: Major-route additional clonal cytogenetic abnormalities at diagnosis or acquired on treatment are a hallmark criterion of accelerated-phase CML.
CML accelerated phase includes 10%-19% blasts in peripheral blood or bone marrow.
CML blast phase is defined by at least 20% blasts in peripheral blood or bone marrow.
CML accelerated phase includes peripheral-blood basophils at least 20%.
Myeloid sarcoma (extramedullary blast proliferation) qualifies as CML blast phase.

CML accelerated phase includes specified additional clonal cytogenetic abnormalities in Philadelphia-positive cells: second Ph, trisomy 8, isochromosome 17q, trisomy 19, complex karyotype, or 3q26.2 abnormalities.
A JAK2 V617F VAF below 1% should prompt a search for coexisting canonical CALR and MPL mutations.
Highly sensitive detection of JAK2 V617F/JAK2 exon 12, MPL W515L/K, and CALR supports classification of PV, ET, or PMF and distinguishes molecularly wild-type/triple-negative cases.
In JAK2 exon 12-mutated PV with isolated erythrocytosis and erythroid-predominant marrow, the usual panmyelosis criterion may not apply.
JAK2 exon 12-mutated PV is prognostically similar to JAK2 V617F-mutated PV.
Absence of a CSF3R mutation does not by itself exclude CNL.
Activating CSF3R mutations are the diagnostic genetic signature of CNL.
For PV, highly sensitive JAK2 V617F testing below 1% sensitivity is recommended; if negative, noncanonical/atypical JAK2 exon 12-15 mutations should be considered.
In sustained absolute erythrocytosis above the specified higher hemoglobin/hematocrit thresholds, marrow biopsy may be unnecessary when JAK2 V617F or JAK2 exon 12 mutation is present.
JAK2, CALR, or MPL mutation is an ET major diagnostic criterion.
JAK2 V617F or JAK2 exon 12 mutation is a PV major diagnostic criterion.
Sensitive JAK2 V617F, CALR, and MPL testing is recommended in PMF; negative cases should be assessed for noncanonical JAK2/MPL mutations.
Detection of mutations such as ASXL1, EZH2, IDH1, IDH2, SF3B1, SRSF2, or TET2 supports the clonal nature of suspected PMF when canonical MPN drivers are absent.
In PMF with monocytosis, a higher VAF of MPN-driver mutations supports PMF with monocytosis rather than CMML.
CNL requires peripheral-blood WBC at least 13×10^9/L when an activating CSF3R mutation is present; the threshold is at least 25×10^9/L when such a mutation is absent.
CSF3R T618I or another activating CSF3R mutation satisfies the molecular component of CNL criterion 3.
In the absence of an activating CSF3R mutation, CNL requires persistent neutrophilia for at least 3 months, splenomegaly, and no identifiable reactive cause.
CNL requires that diagnostic criteria for BCR::ABL1-positive CML not be met.
For pre-PMF and overt PMF, a JAK2, CALR, or MPL mutation, another clonal marker, or absence of reactive fibrosis satisfies the second major criterion.
Overt PMF major morphology criterion is megakaryocytic proliferation and atypia with reticulin and/or collagen fibrosis grade 2 or 3.

Pre-PMF major morphology criterion is megakaryocytic proliferation and atypia with fibrosis grade <2, increased age-adjusted marrow cellularity, granulocytic proliferation, and often decreased erythropoiesis.
Pre-PMF or overt PMF requires all three major criteria plus at least one minor criterion confirmed on two consecutive determinations.
CNL accelerated phase is defined by 10%-19% blasts in blood or marrow.
CNL blast phase is defined by at least 20% blasts in blood or marrow.

When no clonal cytogenetic/molecular abnormality or increased blasts are present, supportive marrow findings can suffice for CEL, NOS if persistent eosinophilia is present and other causes are excluded.
CEL, NOS requires peripheral-blood eosinophils at least 1.5×10^9/L and at least 10% of WBC.
CEL, NOS requires <20% blasts in peripheral blood and marrow and must not meet another AML-defining criterion.
CEL, NOS requires absence of BCR::ABL1, other ABL1, PDGFRA, PDGFRB, FGFR1, JAK2, and FLT3 tyrosine-kinase fusions.

CEL, NOS marrow shows increased cellularity with dysplastic megakaryocytes, with or without other-lineage dysplasia and often fibrosis, with an eosinophilic infiltrate; alternatively increased blasts can satisfy the specified marrow/blood thresholds.
CEL, NOS requires demonstration of a clonal cytogenetic abnormality and/or somatic mutation.
The ICC diagnosis of CEL, NOS requires all six listed criteria.
MPN-U requires clinical and hematologic features of an MPN.
MPN-U requires JAK2, CALR, or MPL mutation or another clonal marker.
MPN-U requires that criteria for BCR::ABL1-positive CML not be met.
MPN-U requires that criteria for any other MPN, MDS, or MDS/MPN not be met.
Sensitive JAK2 V617F, CALR, and MPL assays are recommended in MPN-U; noncanonical JAK2/MPL mutations should be sought if canonical drivers are negative.
Mutations such as ASXL1, EZH2, IDH1, IDH2, SF3B1, SRSF2, and TET2 can support clonality in MPN-U.
For MDS/MPN, anemia is hemoglobin <13 g/dL in males or <12 g/dL in females.
For MDS/MPN, neutropenia is ANC <1.8×10^9/L.
For MDS/MPN, thrombocytopenia is platelets <150×10^9/L.
ICC MDS/MPN disorders generally require cytopenia together with a proliferative cytosis.
CMML-1 is defined by <5% blasts/promonocytes in peripheral blood and <10% in bone marrow.
CMML-2 is defined by 5%-19% blasts/promonocytes in blood, 10%-19% in marrow, or the presence of Auer rods.
ICC eliminates the CMML-0 subtype.
CMML-associated mutations in splicing, epigenetic, signaling, and transcriptional genes can establish clonality and are expected in most cases with modern sequencing.
CMML requires absolute monocytes at least 0.5×10^9/L and at least 10% of the WBC.
CMML requires blasts, including promonocytes, to comprise <20% of blood and marrow cells.
CMML clonality is established by abnormal cytogenetics and/or at least one myeloid-neoplasm-associated mutation at allele frequency at least 10%.

Without demonstrable clonality, CMML requires monocytes at least 1.0×10^9/L and >10% of WBC plus increased blasts (≥5% marrow and/or ≥2% blood), morphologic dysplasia, or a CMML-consistent abnormal immunophenotype.
CMML marrow examination should show CMML-consistent myeloid/monocytic proliferation and lack diagnostic features of AML, MPN, or another monocytosis-associated condition.
CMML requires absence of BCR::ABL1.
CMML requires absence of genetic abnormalities defining M/LN-eo with tyrosine-kinase fusions.
Acquisition/presence of NPM1 mutation in established CMML should be noted but does not by itself define de novo AML.
ASXL1 mutation in CMML has prognostic implications.
NPM1-mutated CMML is associated with a particularly aggressive clinical course and rapid progression to acute leukemia.
With clonality present, ICC lowers the CMML absolute-monocyte threshold to at least 0.5×10^9/L while retaining the requirement that monocytes comprise at least 10% of WBC.
The myeloproliferative subtype of CMML (CMML-MP) is defined by WBC >13×10^9/L.
Absence of JAK2, CALR, and MPL driver mutations supports aCML, whereas a history of MPN and/or these driver mutations tends to exclude aCML.
CSF3R mutation is uncommon in aCML and, if detected, should trigger careful morphologic review for CNL.
SETBP1 mutation, often with co-mutated ASXL1, supports a diagnosis of aCML.
aCML requires eosinophils below 10% of WBC; hypereosinophilia is incompatible with the diagnosis.
Cytopenia used for clonal cytopenias/MDS should be acquired, sustained, and not explained by another condition.

Certain genetic abnormalities remain MDS-defining in persistent cytopenia irrespective of morphologic dysplasia.
Monocytes at least 10% of leukocytes and absolute monocytes at least 0.5×10^9/L at initial presentation exclude MDS and warrant MDS/MPN or MPN classification.
Persistent platelets at least 450×10^9/L at initial presentation exclude MDS except in MDS with del(5q) or inv(3)/t(3;3) and otherwise warrant MDS/MPN or MPN classification.
Persistent unexplained WBC at least 13×10^9/L at initial presentation excludes MDS and warrants MDS/MPN or MPN classification.
The prior MDS with ring sideroblasts entity is replaced by MDS with SF3B1 mutation.
Ring sideroblasts are not required to diagnose MDS-SF3B1 when the molecular and other ICC criteria are met.
Excess blasts supersede other lower-blast MDS subtypes except MDS with mutated TP53.
Patients with MDS/AML should be eligible for both MDS and AML clinical trials.
Complex karyotype without a TP53 mutation does not qualify as TP53-mutated MDS, even with 17p deletion.
Monoallelic TP53 mutation alone is not included in the MDS with mutated TP53 entity.
Monoallelic somatic TP53 mutation is permitted in MDS/AML and AML with mutated TP53 when the other criteria are met.
Complex-karyotype MDS without TP53 mutation has superior prognosis to TP53-mutated MDS and does not belong to the TP53-mutated category.
Monoallelic TP53 mutation in MDS has a less adverse prognostic effect than multi-hit TP53.
Monoallelic TP53-mutated AML has poor prognosis.
Multi-hit TP53 in cytopenic myeloid neoplasms is associated with highly aggressive disease and short survival.
The poor prognosis of MDS with multi-hit TP53 does not appear to depend on blast percentage.
MDS, MDS/AML, and AML with TP53 mutation are grouped across the blast spectrum because of similar aggressive behavior, supporting a more unified treatment strategy.
An established MDS that acquires TP53 mutation can progress to TP53-mutated MDS, MDS/AML, or AML according to blast count and should be designated accordingly.

Any underlying germline predisposition mutation or syndrome should be specified as a qualifier after the MDS diagnosis and subtype.
Therapy-related status is a diagnostic qualifier applied after morphologic/genetic MDS, AML, or MDS/AML classification rather than a stand-alone disease category.

Mutations in ASXL1, BCOR, EZH2, RUNX1, SF3B1, SRSF2, STAG2, U2AF1, or ZRSR2 qualify AML/MDS-AML as myelodysplasia-related gene-mutated after higher-priority defining categories are excluded.

TP53 mutation defines a distinctly aggressive AML category and generally predicts worse prognosis even when overlapping another genetic AML category.

MDS cases with 10%-19% blasts are diagnosed as MDS/AML and are subclassified as MDS/AML with mutated TP53, myelodysplasia-related gene mutations, myelodysplasia-related cytogenetic abnormalities, or MDS/AML, NOS.
Most recurrent-genetic AML categories require at least 10% blasts/blast equivalents; remaining AML categories retain the at least 20% blast requirement.
In-frame bZIP CEBPA mutation defines the favorable-prognosis CEBPA AML entity.
After excluding other defined genetic AML categories, remaining cases are classified as AML, NOS.
Pure erythroid leukemia is typically TP53-mutated and is classified within AML with TP53 mutation.
Single-gene mutation or gene-fusion AML categories take precedence over myelodysplasia-related gene-mutation and myelodysplasia-related cytogenetic groups.

cards.interpretation: An in-frame mutation affecting the CEBPA bZIP region defines the CEBPA-mutated AML subtype whether monoallelic or biallelic.
In-frame CEBPA bZIP mutations are associated with favorable outcome irrespective of monoallelic or biallelic occurrence.
A pathogenic TP53 mutation with variant allele fraction of at least 10%, with or without loss of the wild-type allele, defines AML with mutated TP53.
TP53-mutant AML and MDS are associated with a very poor prognosis.
In the absence of TP53 mutation, mutations in ASXL1, BCOR, EZH2, RUNX1, SF3B1, SRSF2, STAG2, U2AF1, and/or ZRSR2 define AML with myelodysplasia-related gene mutations irrespective of prior MDS.
Myelodysplasia-related gene mutations in ASXL1, BCOR, EZH2, RUNX1, SF3B1, SRSF2, STAG2, U2AF1, and/or ZRSR2 confer adverse prognosis even in de novo AML.

AML with recurrent genetic abnormalities takes precedence over all other AML categories. Among the remaining categories, AML with mutated TP53 takes precedence over AML with myelodysplasia-related gene mutations, which takes precedence over AML with myelodysplasia-related cytogenetic abnormalities. AML with myelodysplasia-related cytogenetic abnormalities is defined, in the absence of higher-priority AML-defining categories, by a qualifying complex karyotype or del(5q)/t(5q)/add(5q), −7/del(7q), +8, del(12p)/t(12p)/add(12p), i(17q), −17/add(17p)/del(17p), del(20q), and/or idic(X)(q13).
Germline predisposition should be considered in patients with hematopoietic malignancy regardless of age; DDX41 predisposition alleles can present at older ages.
Because allogeneic HCT and related-donor selection may be relevant in AML, germline risk-allele testing should be performed as early as possible during clinical management.
If conventional cytogenetics fails, FISH is an alternative for detecting RUNX1::RUNX1T1, CBFB::MYH11, KMT2A, and MECOM fusions and selected myelodysplasia-related chromosome abnormalities.
